claim: DNA methylation is an essential epigenetic mark
source: DNA methylation is an essential (Li et al., 1992) epigenetic mark whose role in gene regulation and its dependency on genomic sequence and environment is not yet fully understood (Jones, 2012; Schubeler, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 1992

claim: The role of DNA methylation in gene regulation and its dependency on genomic sequence and environment are not fully understood
source: DNA methylation is an essential (Li et al., 1992) epigenetic mark whose role in gene regulation and its dependency on genomic sequence and environment is not yet fully understood (Jones, 2012; Schubeler, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jones, 2012 and Schubeler, 2012

claim: DNA methylation in vertebrates occurs most commonly in cytosines that are adjacent to guanines (CpG sites)
source: DNA methylation in vertebrates occurs most commonly in cytosines that are adjacent to guanines (CpG sites).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DNA methylation

claim: Mammalian DNA methylation levels are generally high
source: Mammalian DNA methylation levels are generally high, although CpG rich regions, called CpG islands (CGI), appear mostly unmethylated (Bird, 2002; Weber et al., 2007; Lister et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bird, 2002; Weber et al., 2007; Lister et al., 2009

claim: CpG islands appear mostly unmethylated
source: Mammalian DNA methylation levels are generally high, although CpG rich regions, called CpG islands (CGI), appear mostly unmethylated (Bird, 2002; Weber et al., 2007; Lister et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bird, 2002; Weber et al., 2007; Lister et al., 2009

claim: The mechanisms of de novo methylation and maintenance of methylation patterns are well known
source: The mechanisms of de novo methylation and maintenance of methylation patterns are well known (Shoemaker et al., 2011), and alterations of these can cause severe diseases (Robertson, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shoemaker et al., 2011

claim: Alterations of DNA methylation mechanisms can cause severe diseases
source: The mechanisms of de novo methylation and maintenance of methylation patterns are well known (Shoemaker et al., 2011), and alterations of these can cause severe diseases (Robertson, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Robertson, 2005

claim: DNA methylation was originally reported to be involved in gene silencing
source: Even though it was originally reported to be involved in gene silencing (Holliday and Pugh, 1975; Riggs, 1975), more recent studies have found that DNA methylation can also be positively correlated to gene transcription when found in gene bodies (Hellman and Chess, 2007; Lister et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Holliday and Pugh, 1975; Riggs, 1975

claim: DNA methylation can be positively correlated to gene transcription when found in gene bodies
source: Even though it was originally reported to be involved in gene silencing (Holliday and Pugh, 1975; Riggs, 1975), more recent studies have found that DNA methylation can also be positively correlated to gene transcription when found in gene bodies (Hellman and Chess, 2007; Lister et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hellman and Chess, 2007; Lister et al., 2009

claim: DNA methylation participates in gene expression by marking alternative intra-genic promoters
source: Additionally, its participation in gene expression is proving to be highly variable, ranging from marking alternative intra-genic promoters (Maunakea et al., 2010), to being affected by transcription factors (TFs) at enhancers (Stadler et al., 2011) or it-self affecting the binding of TFs such as MYC (Prendergast and Ziff, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maunakea et al., 2010

claim: DNA methylation is affected by transcription factors at enhancers
source: Additionally, its participation in gene expression is proving to be highly variable, ranging from marking alternative intra-genic promoters (Maunakea et al., 2010), to being affected by transcription factors (TFs) at enhancers (Stadler et al., 2011) or it-self affecting the binding of TFs such as MYC (Prendergast and Ziff, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stadler et al., 2011

claim: DNA methylation affects the binding of transcription factors such as MYC
source: Additionally, its participation in gene expression is proving to be highly variable, ranging from marking alternative intra-genic promoters (Maunakea et al., 2010), to being affected by transcription factors (TFs) at enhancers (Stadler et al., 2011) or it-self affecting the binding of TFs such as MYC (Prendergast and Ziff, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prendergast and Ziff, 1991

claim: Whether DNA methylation plays a passive or an active role in gene regulation remains a topic of debate
source: Hence, whether DNA methylation is a consequence of gene regulation, or whether it controls gene expression changes—that is, whether it plays a passive or an active role in gene regulation—still remains a topic of debate (Schubeler, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schubeler, 2012

claim: DNA methylation can be affected by environment
source: Additionally, DNA methylation can be affected by environment (Kaminsky et al., 2009) but it has also been proven that regions in the genome can autonomously determine DNA methylation states (Lienert et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaminsky et al., 2009

claim: Regions in the genome can autonomously determine DNA methylation states
source: Additionally, DNA methylation can be affected by environment (Kaminsky et al., 2009) but it has also been proven that regions in the genome can autonomously determine DNA methylation states (Lienert et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lienert et al., 2010

claim: Genetic variation influences DNA methylation levels in different cell-types
source: Furthermore, studies looking at natural DNA methylation variation in human populations have shown that genetic variation influences DNA methylation levels in different cell-types (Gibbs et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010; Bell et al., 2011), but the mechanisms by which this occurs are far from clear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gibbs et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010; Bell et al., 2011

claim: The association between DNA methylation and gene expression in a population context has been reported to be both positive and negative
source: In these and other studies (Kulis et al., 2012), the association between DNA methylation and gene expression in a population context, where the same gene and same methylation site can be compared across multiple individuals, has been reported to be both positive and negative.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kulis et al., 2012

claim: The GenCord collection consists of umbilical cord samples from 204 newborn babies of central European descent
source: We use the GenCord collection (Dimas et al., 2009) of umbilical cord samples from 204 newborn babies of central European descent, from which we derived three cell-types: fibroblasts (primary cells), T-cells (primary cells) and lymphoblastoid cells (immortalized cell lines, LCLs) (Figure 1).
evidence: Described in the methods and shown in Figure 1

claim: Three cell-types were derived from the GenCord samples: fibroblasts, T-cells, and lymphoblastoid cells
source: We use the GenCord collection (Dimas et al., 2009) of umbilical cord samples from 204 newborn babies of central European descent, from which we derived three cell-types: fibroblasts (primary cells), T-cells (primary cells) and lymphoblastoid cells (immortalized cell lines, LCLs) (Figure 1).
evidence: Described in the methods and shown in Figure 1

claim: Each individual was genotyped for 2.5 million SNPs
source: We genotyped each individual for 2.5 million SNPs, and sequenced the poly-A transcriptome of all three cell-types from the 204 individuals yielding a median of 16 million exonic reads per sample.
evidence: Described in the methods section

claim: The poly-A transcriptome of all three cell-types was sequenced yielding a median of 16 million exonic reads per sample
source: We genotyped each individual for 2.5 million SNPs, and sequenced the poly-A transcriptome of all three cell-types from the 204 individuals yielding a median of 16 million exonic reads per sample.
evidence: Described in the methods section

claim: Samples from 18 to 21 genetic or expression outliers were removed
source: We subsequently removed samples from 18 to 21 genetic or expression outliers, yielding a final set of 183–186 individuals per cell type (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Described in the methods and shown in Figure 1 supplements

claim: The final set consisted of 183-186 individuals per cell type
source: We subsequently removed samples from 18 to 21 genetic or expression outliers, yielding a final set of 183–186 individuals per cell type (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Described in the methods and shown in Figure 1 supplements

claim: The assayed SNPs were imputed to the Phase 1 release of the 1000 genomes project yielding a set of 6.9 million SNPs
source: The assayed SNPs were imputed to the Phase 1 release of the 1000 genomes project (Abecasis et al., 2012) yielding a set of 6.9 million SNPs.
evidence: Described in the methods section with citation to 1000 genomes project

claim: Normalized expression levels were obtained for 70,800-76,870 exons belonging to 12,265-12,863 genes
source: We obtained normalized expression levels for 70,800–76,870 exons belonging to 12,265–12,863 genes (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Described in the methods and shown in Figure 1 supplements

claim: DNA methylation levels were measured using bisulfite-conversion and hybridization to a bead chip, assaying 416,118 CpG sites in 66-118 samples
source: DNA methylation levels were measured using bisulfite-conversion and hybridization to a bead chip, assaying 416,118 CpG sites in 66–118 samples.
evidence: Described in the methods section

claim: Normalized methylation levels of CpG sites range from 0 to 1, reflecting the percentage of methylation per site
source: Normalized methylation levels of CpG sites range from 0 to 1, reflecting the percentage of methylation per site (β-value; Figure 1—figure supplements 5–7).
evidence: Described in the methods and shown in Figure 1 supplements

claim: At 10% FDR, 2115-3372 expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) were identified using a 1 Mb window to either side of the TSS
source: At 10% FDR, we identify 2115–3372 expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) using a 1 Mb window to either side of the TSS.
evidence: Results from the association analysis described in the manuscript

claim: 14,189-32,318 methylation QTLs (mQTLs) were discovered using a 5-kb window to either side of the CpG site
source: We discover 14,189–32,318 methylation QTLs (mQTLs) using a 5-kb window to either side of the CpG site.
evidence: Results from the association analysis described in the manuscript

claim: 1541-17,267 significant expression to methylation associations (eQTMs) were found using a 50-kb window around the TSS
source: We find 1541–17,267 significant expression to methylation associations (eQTMs) using a 50-kb window around the TSS; these pertain to 596–3838 genes and 970–6846 CpG sites (Table 1, Figure 1).
evidence: Results from the association analysis described in the manuscript and shown in Table 1

claim: DNA methylation at promoter regions correlates negatively with gene expression levels when looking at comparisons across genes
source: DNA methylation at promoter regions is widely known to correlate negatively with gene expression levels when looking at comparisons across genes (Jones, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jones, 2012

claim: The same pattern of negative correlation between promoter methylation and gene expression is observed in the GenCord study
source: We observe the same pattern in our study looking at the promoter regions of all genes of each individual separately and for each cell-type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2 supplement 1

claim: Methylation sites in promoter regions from positive and negative eQTMs both correlate negatively with gene expression across genes
source: Contrary to our hypothesis, we find that methylation sites correlate negatively with gene expression across genes independently of whether they correlate positively or negatively with gene expression across individuals (Figure 2A; Spearman correlation coefficient, rho = −0.11, p=1.1 × 10−4, and rho = −0.10, p=1.7 × 10−13, respectively; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A with statistical analysis

claim: The mechanisms underlying inter-individual DNA methylation variation associated to gene expression are at least partly independent of the mechanisms involved in the establishment of the repressive mark of promoter DNA methylation across genes during development and differentiation
source: These results suggest that the mechanisms and processes underlying inter-individual DNA methylation variation associated to gene expression are at least partly independent of the mechanisms involved in the establishment of the repressive mark of promoter DNA methylation across genes during development and differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing that positive and negative eQTMs both correlate negatively with expression across genes

claim: As the level of cell-type methylation differentiation increases, a larger proportion of sites are associated to gene expression (eQTMs)
source: We find that as differentiation per methylation site increases, a higher proportion of eQTMs and mQTLs are observed (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B

claim: As the level of cell-type methylation differentiation increases, a larger proportion of sites are affected by genetic variation (mQTLs)
source: We find that as differentiation per methylation site increases, a higher proportion of eQTMs and mQTLs are observed (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B

claim: The tissue differentiation level of methylation sites involved in eQTMs is significantly higher than for non-eQTM sites
source: This is statistically supported by the fact that the tissue differentiation level of methylation sites involved in eQTMs and mQTLs is significantly higher than for non-eQTM and non-mQTL sites, respectively (all p values<2.2 × 10−16, Wilcoxon test, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: Statistical test results shown in Figure 2 supplement 3

claim: The tissue differentiation level of methylation sites involved in mQTLs is significantly higher than for non-mQTL sites
source: This is statistically supported by the fact that the tissue differentiation level of methylation sites involved in eQTMs and mQTLs is significantly higher than for non-eQTM and non-mQTL sites, respectively (all p values<2.2 × 10−16, Wilcoxon test, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: Statistical test results shown in Figure 2 supplement 3

claim: The establishment of differentially methylated regions during development could be delineating a backbone where local inter-individual changes may occur
source: These results show that the same methylation sites marking or contributing to tissue differentiation are participating in inter-individual variability that is highly determined by genetic variation and associated to gene expression. This could indicate that the establishment of differentially methylated regions during development could be delineating a backbone where local inter-individual changes may occur.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that differentiated sites are more likely to be eQTMs and mQTLs

claim: There is a significant increased presence of negative compared to positive eQTMs in CTCF binding sites, enhancers and promoters
source: We find a significant increased presence of negative compared to positive eQTMs in CTCF binding sites, enhancers and promoters, with this increase being higher in non-CpG island (CGI) promoters compared to CGI promoters (Figure 2C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2C

claim: There is a significant depletion of mQTLs in CGI promoters
source: Interestingly, we discover a significant depletion of mQTLs in CGI promoters, and a significant enrichment of mQTLs in non-CGI promoters (Figure 2D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2D

claim: There is a significant enrichment of mQTLs in non-CGI promoters
source: Interestingly, we discover a significant depletion of mQTLs in CGI promoters, and a significant enrichment of mQTLs in non-CGI promoters (Figure 2D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2D

claim: Methylation sites in non-CGI promoters are under a stronger genetic control than at CGI promoters
source: This shows that methylation sites in non-CGI promoters are under a stronger genetic control than at CGI promoters, where methylation is in general robustly maintained at low levels.
evidence: Inferred from the enrichment of mQTLs in non-CGI promoters and depletion in CGI promoters

claim: Genetic variation in CpG islands commonly affects gene expression
source: Nevertheless, genetic variation in CpG islands commonly affects gene expression, since we find that eQTLs are significantly enriched at these genomic regions (all p values<0.03).
evidence: Statistical test results reported in the text

claim: The role of DNA methylation can be highly dependent on the genomic and functional context
source: Overall, these results suggest that the role of DNA methylation can be highly dependent on the genomic and functional context.
evidence: Inferred from the context-specific patterns of eQTMs and mQTLs

claim: At a genome-wide level a significantly greater allelic imbalance is associated with heterozygote eQTLs in all three cell-types
source: Similar to other studies (Dimas et al., 2009; Pickrell et al., 2010; Montgomery et al., 2010), at a genome-wide level a significantly greater allelic imbalance is associated with heterozygote eQTLs in all three cell-types (p values<3.0 × 10−8, Figure 3A).
evidence: Statistical test results shown in Figure 3A and supported by citations

claim: A comparison of allelic imbalance between individuals with semimethylated eQTMs and homomethylated eQTMs revealed no significant differences
source: A comparison of allelic imbalance between individuals with semimethylated eQTMs, and homomethylated (i.e., fully methylated, β-value > 0.7, or unmethylated, β-value < 0.3) eQTMs, revealed no significant differences (p values>0.42, Figure 3A).
evidence: Statistical test results shown in Figure 3A

claim: ASE driven by heterozygote eQTLs is significantly higher than that of semimethylated eQTMs
source: Additionally, ASE driven by heterozygote eQTLs is significantly higher than that of semimethylated eQTMs (p values<7.5 × 10−3, Figure 3A).
evidence: Statistical test results shown in Figure 3A

claim: Allelic imbalance in imprinted genes is significantly higher than in homomethylated eQTMs
source: Furthermore, as a positive control, we observe that allelic imbalance in imprinted genes, known to be driven by allelic DNA methylation, is significantly higher than in homomethylated eQTMs (p values<9.7 × 10−4, Figure 3A).
evidence: Statistical test results shown in Figure 3A

claim: There is no evidence of methylation alone contributing to ASE in the absence of genetic variation
source: Thus, while ASE is shown to be significantly driven by genetic variation (or by DNA methylation in imprinted genes), we find no evidence in our data of methylation alone contributing to ASE.
evidence: Based on the analysis of allelic imbalance in relation to methylation status

claim: DNA methylation is rarely allele-specific in the absence of DNA sequence variation effects
source: This argues that DNA methylation is rarely allele-specific in the absence of DNA sequence variation effects, and while we cannot exclude other possible epigenetic sources of ASE, the results suggest that the widespread ASE across the genome may be primarily driven by common and rare genetic regulatory variants.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of association between semimethylated sites and allelic imbalance

claim: Widespread ASE across the genome may be primarily driven by common and rare genetic regulatory variants
source: This argues that DNA methylation is rarely allele-specific in the absence of DNA sequence variation effects, and while we cannot exclude other possible epigenetic sources of ASE, the results suggest that the widespread ASE across the genome may be primarily driven by common and rare genetic regulatory variants.
evidence: Inferred from the strong association between heterozygote eQTLs and allelic imbalance

claim: Synergistic interactions between genetic variants and DNA methylation on gene expression are enriched in LCLs and T-cells
source: Synergistic interactions are enriched in LCLs and T-cells (Figure 3B) with π1 being 4.3% and 9.3% (all p<0.001), which reflects the percent of estimated true positives from the p value distributions (Storey and Tibshirani, 2003).
evidence: Statistical test results shown in Figure 3B

claim: In fibroblasts, the observed π1 is 12.4%, 7.2 times larger than the top permuted π1, suggesting a significant enrichment of interactions
source: In fibroblasts, although the p value distribution is not above the 95th confidence limit (Figure 3B), the observed π1 is 12.4% (p<0.001), 7.2 times larger than the top permuted π1, which suggests a significant enrichment of interactions.
evidence: Statistical test results shown in Figure 3B

claim: 3, 91 and 14 individually significant interactions were found in fibroblasts, LCLs and T-cells, respectively, at 10% false discovery rate
source: Finally, we find 3, 91 and 14 individually significant interactions in fibroblasts, LCLs and T-cells, respectively, at 10% false discovery rate (FDR).
evidence: Statistical test results reported in the text

claim: The results reflect the interdependency of genetic and epigenetic variation to determine gene expression levels
source: Overall, these results reflect the interdependency of genetic and epigenetic variation to determine gene expression levels.
evidence: Inferred from the enrichment of synergistic interactions

claim: All three causative models (INDEP, SME, and SEM) occur, depending on cell-type and sign of correlation between DNA methylation and gene expression
source: All three models occur, depending on cell-type and sign of correlation between DNA methylation and gene expression (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4 supplement 1A

claim: The INDEP model, that reflects a passive role for DNA methylation, is the most likely model in fibroblasts and LCLs
source: The INDEP model, that reflects a passive role for DNA methylation, is the most likely model in fibroblasts and LCLs.
evidence: Based on Bayesian network analysis results

claim: In T-cells the SME model, where methylation takes an active causative role, is the major contributor
source: However, in T-cells the SME model, where methylation takes an active causative role, is the major contributor.
evidence: Based on Bayesian network analysis results

claim: In the SEM model, where methylation is passive being influenced by gene expression levels, a higher likelihood of pos-eQTMs is found compared to the SME model
source: Note that in the SEM model, where methylation is passive being influenced by gene expression levels, a higher likelihood of pos-eQTMs is found compared to the SME model.
evidence: Based on Bayesian network analysis results

claim: DNA methylation can be both active, by being a likely cause of gene expression variation levels, or passive, by being a consequence or an independent mark of gene expression levels
source: Overall, these results suggest that DNA methylation can be both active, by being a likely cause of gene expression variation levels, or passive, by being a consequence or an independent mark of gene expression levels.
evidence: Inferred from the Bayesian network analysis showing all three models occur

claim: Transcription factors can influence DNA methylation levels near their binding sites in mice
source: It has been shown in mice (Stadler et al., 2011) that TFs can influence DNA methylation levels near their binding sites (TFBSs).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stadler et al., 2011

claim: By correlating expression levels of TFs with DNA methylation at their TFBSs in different cell-types, this pattern has also been observed for some TFs in human tissues
source: In addition, by correlating expression levels of TFs with DNA methylation at their TFBSs in different cell-types, this pattern has also been observed for some TFs in human tissues (Thurman et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thurman et al., 2012

claim: There is a strong enrichment of significant TF-methylation associations, with π1 being 18%, 9% and 25%, in fibroblasts, LCL, and T-cells, respectively
source: We found a strong enrichment of significant TF-methylation associations, with π1 being 18%, 9% and 25%, in fibroblasts, LCL, and T-cells, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical test results shown in Figure 4 supplement 2

claim: At 10% FDR, significant associations were found for 27, 47 and 99 different TFs in fibroblasts, LCL and T-cells, respectively
source: At 10% FDR, we find significant associations for 27, 47 and 99 different TFs in fibroblasts, LCL and T-cells, respectively.
evidence: Statistical test results reported in the text

claim: There is an enrichment of low p values for interactions between genetic variants and TF abundance on DNA methylation levels, with π1 estimated at 15% of true positives
source: Despite the limited number of cases that could be tested (N = 114), we find an enrichment of low p values for such interactions, with π1 estimated at 15% of true positives, and the top interaction involving the TF c-Jun in T-cells (p=1 × 10−4, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Statistical test results shown in Figure 4 supplement 3

claim: TF levels could be influencing DNA methylation and gene expression levels simultaneously
source: These results suggest that TF levels could be influencing DNA methylation and gene expression levels simultaneously.
evidence: Inferred from the enrichment of TF-methylation associations

claim: In some cases TF influence on methylation and expression could occur via the interaction with DNA sequence variation
source: It is possible that in some cases this could occur via the interaction with DNA sequence variation.
evidence: Inferred from the enrichment of interactions between SNPs and TF abundance on methylation

claim: Inter-individual DNA methylation changes are mechanistically associated to genetic variation and gene expression in complex and context dependent ways that can be of passive or active nature
source: In this study, we have shown that inter-individual DNA methylation changes are mechanistically associated to genetic variation and gene expression in complex and context dependent ways that can be of passive or active nature.
evidence: Summary of the findings from the study

claim: DNA methylation levels can depend on TF binding
source: DNA methylation levels can depend on TF binding (Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stadler et al., 2011

claim: TF binding levels can be determined by both inter-individual differences of TF abundance and genetic variants at their binding sites
source: TF binding levels in turn can be determined by both inter-individual differences of TF abundance and genetic variants at their binding sites.
evidence: Inferred from the study's findings on TF-methylation associations and SNP-TF interactions

claim: DNA methylation can be linked to genetic variation and can participate in gene regulation in a passive manner
source: This picture shows how DNA methylation can be linked to genetic variation, and can participate in gene regulation in a passive manner.
evidence: Inferred from the study's findings on the INDEP model and TF-methylation associations

claim: Non-genetically determined DNA methylation is rarely allelic but rather defined at the whole cell level
source: Additionally, our results suggest that non-genetically determined DNA methylation is rarely allelic but rather defined at the whole cell level.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of association between semimethylated sites and allelic imbalance

claim: When a population of cells is observed to be semimethylated the most likely scenario is that only a fraction of the cells are fully methylated rather than one of the alleles in each of the cells is methylated
source: That is, when we observe a population of cells to be semimethylated the most likely scenario is that only a fraction of the cells are fully methylated rather than one of the alleles in each of the cells is methylated.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of association between semimethylated sites and allelic imbalance

claim: Methylation sites that represent a repressive state with respect to tissue differentiation can also participate in positive and negative associations with gene expression when looking at inter-individual variability
source: Further, we show that methylation sites that represent a repressive state with respect to tissue differentiation can also participate in positive and negative associations with gene expression when looking at inter-individual variability.
evidence: Based on the finding that promoter methylation sites can be both positive and negative eQTMs

claim: DNA methylation as a whole emerges both as marker and determinant of cellular identity
source: DNA methylation as a whole emerges both as marker and determinant of cellular identity and may provide a platform by which genetic variation and other variable factors among individuals (e.g., TFs) exert their effect to differentially influence cellular processes.
evidence: Inferred from the study's findings on the relationship between differentiation, eQTMs, and mQTLs

claim: DNA methylation may provide a platform by which genetic variation and other variable factors among individuals exert their effect to differentially influence cellular processes
source: DNA methylation as a whole emerges both as marker and determinant of cellular identity and may provide a platform by which genetic variation and other variable factors among individuals (e.g., TFs) exert their effect to differentially influence cellular processes.
evidence: Inferred from the study's findings on the relationship between differentiation, eQTMs, mQTLs, and TF-methylation associations
